title: The Sefat Emet's inner point
hook: the Sefat Emet taught that every person has an inner point that stays pure
carry: the inner point: covered, never stained
tomorrow: why would the Torah say God needed refreshing?

segments.voice: Last week ended on Rebbe Elimelech's prayer: pray to see others' virtues, not their faults. This week, a teacher who looked for what's underneath.
screen: `PRAY TO SEE OTHERS' VIRTUES, NOT THEIR FAULTS.`

segments.voice: Saturday morning in a garage: an old door across two sawhorses, a heat gun, a scraper. The first layer of paint curls off mint green. Under it, brown. Under that, a cracked white somebody chose long ago. Then the scraper hits something different: bare wood, grain and knots and all, the wood the door was made of before anyone painted it. A Hasidic teacher, writing on the weekly Torah portion, said a person is built a lot like that door. So what's under all the layers, the part that never got dirty?
screen: `A DOOR ON TWO SAWHORSES.` → `MINT GREEN, BROWN, CRACKED WHITE.` → `THEN, BARE WOOD.`

segments.voice: He's known by the name of his book, the Sefat Emet, the language of truth: Rabbi Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter, the rebbe of Ger. A phrase that runs through his teaching is the nekudah penimit, the inner point. Inside a person, he teaches, there's a point of life from God that stays pure. Mistakes, habits, years of noise can cover it. They can't stain it. That's the answer: under all the layers, the inner point is what never got dirty. For the Sefat Emet this changes what repair looks like. Teshuvah, returning, isn't building a new self from nothing. It's scraping back to the wood that was always there. And it changes what a holy life looks like. The work, in his reading, is to keep that point open and let it shine out into the ordinary week, through prayer, study and the mitzvot, the commandments. Here's what's quietly radical about it. The point is never earned. It doesn't grow when you're good and shrink when you're not. It's simply there, waiting under the paint, on the worst day and the best one. Nobody can take it off you, including you. A parent could say it at bedtime: whatever happened today, the best part of you is still in there, untouched.
screen: `SEFAT EMET: THE LANGUAGE OF TRUTH.` · `A POINT THAT STAYS PURE.` · `TESHUVAH: SCRAPE BACK TO THE WOOD.` · `NEVER EARNED, ALWAYS THERE.` · then, large: `THE INNER POINT: COVERED, NEVER STAINED.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes, or rest them on the floor, and let one hand settle on your chest. Let the day's layers come up one at a time, a worry, a mistake, a part you played, and set each aside like paint lifting off. Then, for the rest of the sit, rest on whatever is left underneath, quiet and plain.
screen: `A HAND ON YOUR CHEST.` · `LAYER BY LAYER.` · `WHAT'S LEFT UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: The inner point: the Sefat Emet's nekudah penimit. A point of life from God at a person's center, which can be covered but never stained.
Hold onto this: the inner point, covered by the day's paint, never stained by it. Rest well.

screen: `DAY 1618 COUNTS.` → `LATER VOICES · 11 OF 40.` → `TOMORROW: WHY WOULD THE TORAH SAY GOD NEEDED REFRESHING?`

howItsDone: The Sefat Emet's teachings on the weekly Torah portion are studied in Ger Hasidism and far beyond it, and his idea of the inner point is often taught alongside teshuvah, especially in the season before Yom Kippur.
